docs.title: Brix
docs.text:
Developers should not have to become build-system experts—or learn a language used only by their build system—just to build their code. They want builds to be easy to describe, fast, correct, and otherwise out of the way.

Brix is a library of building blocks for creating builds in languages people already know—thus the name “Brix.” It currently provides those blocks as an ordinary Python library, backed by a production Rust engine. You can describe anything from a tiny build to a large, complex monorepo without implementing a scheduler, incremental engine, cache, or safety machinery yourself.

You can build TypeScript projects with Brix today, but build definitions must be written in Python. JavaScript/TypeScript build-file authoring is planned but is not supported yet.

docs.title: What Brix gives you
docs.text:
• Fast builds. The performance-sensitive engine is Rust, independent work runs in parallel, and work that does not need to happen is avoided.
  • Incremental builds you can trust. An incremental build must produce what a clean build would, including deleting outputs that should no longer exist.
  • Git-inspired atomic builds. Inspect status, stage a complete build, then commit or discard it without leaving a half-updated workspace.
  • Local and shared caching. Reuse work from another build, workspace, teammate, or CI.
  • Less dependency bookkeeping. Inputs and outputs establish relationships and ordering; C/C++ headers and TypeScript imports can be discovered automatically.
  • Small project to monorepo. Distribute build files at package boundaries and load only the affected portion of a large repository.
  • Explainable and configurable. Compose only the layers a project needs, while status, graph, help, and env explain what Brix sees.

Because Python and JavaScript are widely used and well understood by AI coding assistants, an assistant can help create, explain, and maintain a Brix build. The repository also contains working examples and starter templates to copy instead of beginning with a blank file.

docs.title: A small C++ build
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from brix import Graph, cli, cpp

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

def create_graph() -> Graph:
    graph = Graph()
    data = graph.data
    graph.add(
        cpp.CompileSourceAction(
            source_files=data.glob("src/{name}.cpp"),
            object_files=data.glob("build/{name}.o"),
        ),
        cpp.LinkApplicationAction(
            object_files=data.glob("build/{name}.o"),
            output_file=data.file("build/app"),
        ),
    )
    return graph

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(cli.main(create_graph, root=ROOT))

docs.title: Tenets
docs.text:
These are the principles the design holds to; they explain why the API looks the way it does.

  • Declare inputs and outputs, not order. A step names the data it reads and writes. Brix infers the dependency edges from overlapping data sets and runs independent steps in parallel — you never hand-wire build order. (For the rare case where two steps are ordered without sharing a file, Graph.force_order() is the explicit escape hatch.)

  • An incremental build equals a clean build. A rebuild produces exactly the output state a from-scratch build would — including removing outputs whose source is gone and rebuilding everything downstream of a real change. There is no half-updated tree to reason about.

  • Skip work when the meaning did not change. Content-key lenses compare a file by what dependents actually depend on: a Java jar by its ABI, a TypeScript module by its declared types. An implementation-only edit produces an identical lens digest, so dependents replay instead of rebuilding — while a public-interface change still cascades.

  • One model, many languages. Typed helpers for C++, Java, Kotlin, and TypeScript all lower to the same generic action/data model, so languages compose in a single graph. Correctness features (incrementality, caching, atomic staging) apply uniformly to every language, or to none — never a per-language feature matrix.

  • Refuse loudly rather than ship something stale. Where Brix cannot yet guarantee a result — an atomic staging hazard, a lens that would be unsound for a language — it fails with a clear, identical error instead of silently producing a possibly-wrong build. Correctness outranks cleverness.

  • No surprises in the workspace. status explains what would run and why before you run it; atomic staging means a failed build never partly changes your tree; and planning rejects any graph where two steps could write the same output. A build either completes cleanly or leaves things as they were.

  • Python composes; the engine is shared. You author in ordinary Python. A shared Rust engine owns planning, scheduling, fingerprints, caching, and the performance-critical execution — the same language-neutral contract intended to back other authoring front-ends.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: The API Reference documents the public authoring surface, generated directly from the code. It covers only what you build with — the graph and action model, the typed language helpers, the data expressions, the command-line entry point, and the extension seams — not the engine internals.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
This reference is generated directly from the source docstrings, so it always matches the installed version. It documents only the public authoring surface — what you write build files with. The engine internals (planner, scheduler, incremental metadata, the Rust core) are deliberately not here.

Everything you author against is reachable from the top-level brix package:

from brix import Graph, IncrementalBuilder, cli, cpp, java
Section What's in it Core & builders The graph and action model, the builder/layer stack, reporters, results, and workspace loading. Data model Data expressions — files, globs, values, tools — the inputs and outputs actions declare. C++ · Java · Kotlin · TypeScript · Spring Boot Typed language helpers that lower to the generic model. Command line The cli.main entry point a project's brix.py exposes. Extending brix The plug-in seams: cache stores, content lenses, and change detectors.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
A project's brix.py exposes a command-line interface by calling cli.main. It provides build, status, clean, help, and related subcommands, plus project-defined target aliases and build-then-act commands.

CLI helpers: the command-line section of a project's brix.py.

Brix is a library; the CLI is a thin client over builders, status, and metadata. A project's build file ends with:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(brix.cli.main(create_graph))

Commands (default: build):

brix.py [build] [-j N] [--silent | --quiet-replays] [--stage]
brix.py status      exit 0 = everything fresh, 1 = work pending
brix.py errors      replay last recorded failures; exit 1 if any
brix.py commit      apply staging held by `build --stage`
brix.py discard     throw held/failed staging away
brix.py clean       delete built outputs and metadata
brix.py graph       print the execution plan's structure
brix.py help        show this build file's live configuration
brix.py env         show the last build's environment and what changed

env reports the environment the most recent build ran under and diffs it against the current one (exit 1 if it differs) — the "works on my machine" detective; a build captures it as a side effect (docs/environment-recording.md). help introspects the builder chain (which layers are wired, so whether --stage / commit / discard apply), the target aliases, and the project's commands=, so the effect of build is visible without reading the file. build --stage builds fully but holds outputs in staging for review — the workspace changes only at commit. Requires an atomic builder.

Projects can add build-then-act subcommands via commands= — each builds its targets first, then hands the built paths to a project function (brix.py view wealth → build wealth's video, then play it).

The engine never prints; this module is a client, so printing here is fine — it is the client.

docs.title: Alias dataclass
docs.text:
Alias(target, description='')

A target shorthand that also carries a description for help.

Aliases may be given as plain values ({"app": "app/dist/main.js"}) or, when a one-line explanation is worth surfacing, as {"app": cli.Alias("app/dist/main.js", "the bundled web app")}. The target is a single output path or a list of them, exactly as a bare alias value; only help reads description.

docs.title: main
docs.text:
main(
    graph_supplier,
    root=".",
    argv=None,
    metadata_dir="build/.brix",
    staging_dir="build/staging",
    builder_factory=None,
    aliases=None,
    commands=None,
    env_ignore=None,
)

builder_factory (optional): zero-argument callable returning the builder to use for build — e.g. the full AtomicBuilder(IncrementalBuilder(...)) stack. Defaults to a plain IncrementalBuilder.

aliases (optional): target shorthands — {"wealth": "output/videos/wealth.mpg"} lets users say build wealth.

commands (optional): build-then-act subcommands — {"view": fn} adds brix.py view <target>..., which builds the targets (aliases apply) and, on success, calls fn(paths) with their absolute Paths. fn may return an exit code.

env_ignore (optional): extra environment-variable names/globs to drop from the recorded build environment, on top of the built-in ignore-list of session noise (see brix.environment and brix.py env).

docs.title: Core & builders
docs.text:
The graph and action model you assemble, the builder/layer stack that runs it, and the reporters, results, and workspace loaders around it.

Brix's supported Python authoring and extension API.

Engine implementation types live in their defining modules and are not part of the top-level v1 contract. See docs/python-api.md.

docs.title: Graph
docs.text:
Graph()

A logical build graph.

Holds action declarations. The engine normally infers dependencies from data-set intersections; force_order covers the exceptional case where actions must be ordered without sharing data.

docs.title: force_order
docs.text:
force_order(
    before, after, *, trigger=EdgeTrigger.ON_SUCCESS
)

Require before to finish before after may run.

This is for ordering with no data relationship; ordinary file/data dependencies should remain implicit. Both actions must already have been added to this graph exactly once.

docs.title: ExternalProcessAction
docs.text:
ExternalProcessAction(
    name=None,
    *,
    command_line,
    inputs=None,
    outputs=None,
    env=None,
    env_used=None,
    env_unset=None,
    env_pass=None,
    worker=None,
    depfile=None,
    self_resolved_inputs=(),
    _env_used_snapshot=None
)

Bases: Expandable

A generic external process.

command_line is a template whose {placeholder} names refer to entries in inputs and outputs. Binding placeholders such as {name} inside data-expression paths belong to a separate namespace and are substituted at expansion time, not at command rendering time.

name is diagnostic identity: node labels, echo lines, and process results. It is optional; unnamed actions are labeled by their command template. Named actions will fingerprint/debug better once incremental metadata and caching exist.

docs.title: substitute

substitute(bindings)

Return a concrete copy with bindings applied to name and data paths.

docs.title: ExpandAll
docs.text:
ExpandAll(element_name, collection, child)

Bases: Expandable

Repeated work over a data collection.

Not an opaque loop: this is an unrealized expansion point in the execution plan. Once collection membership is known, it expands into concrete sibling nodes, one per binding of element_name.

The child is any Expandable — a process action, or another ExpandAll for nested repetition (per video, per scene of that video); use distinct element names per level.

docs.title: substitute
docs.text:
substitute(bindings)

Apply outer bindings. If they bind this expansion's own element (target selection does), the expansion collapses to its substituted child — there is nothing left to expand over.

docs.title: Expandable
docs.text:
Bases: Action

Anything an ExpandAll can instantiate per collection member.

Requires a diagnostic label and binding substitute. Both ExternalProcessAction and ExpandAll itself qualify — so expansion points nest: an outer expansion over videos can instantiate an inner expansion over each video's scenes.

docs.title: EdgeTrigger
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

When an edge lets its target proceed.

ON_SUCCESS is the default: the source must be DONE, and a failure cascades a skip. ON_COMPLETION fires whether the source succeeded or failed — for cleanup that must run because its trigger failed.

docs.title: CacheBuilder
docs.text:
CacheBuilder(inner, cache_dir=None, store=None)

Bases: NestableBuilder

Reuse results across workspaces and clean checkouts.

Wraps another builder; the cache layer sits innermost, keyed by the same action_fingerprint the incremental layer records.

Backing store, pick one:

  • cache_dir (default) — the built-in local CacheStore under this directory. Absolute for a cache shared between checkouts, or workspace-relative; keep a relative one under a .brix-prefixed directory (the default) so workspace scans ignore it.
  • store — any object with the CacheStoreProtocol three methods: a remote team cache, or a TwoTierCacheStore fronting one with local disk. An unreachable store degrades to a cache miss (handled in the layer), never a failed build.

Passing both is an error.

docs.title: AtomicBuilder
docs.text:
AtomicBuilder(inner, staging_dir='build/staging')

Either the whole build lands, or nothing on disk changes.

Wraps another builder; its layer sits outermost, so process outputs and (later) cache-restored outputs all pass through staging. It is intentionally not a NestableBuilder — nothing may wrap it (see that class), so it is always the outermost builder.

docs.title: build
docs.text:
build(
    jobs=None,
    reporter=None,
    targets=None,
    hold=False,
    worker_idle_timeout=None,
)

hold=True: build fully but keep outputs in staging for review — the workspace changes only at commit. worker_idle_timeout: see IncrementalBuilder.build.

docs.title: commit
docs.text:
commit()

Apply held staging to the workspace. None if nothing is staged; (files, deletions) otherwise. Raises ValueError on failed-build staging, which must never reach the workspace.

docs.title: discard
docs.text:
discard()

Throw staging away, workspace untouched. None if nothing is staged; the number of files discarded otherwise.

docs.title: NestableBuilder
docs.text:
Marker for a builder another layer may legally wrap.

AtomicBuilder is deliberately not a NestableBuilder: its layer establishes the staging overlay and its build() carries the P0 staging hazard guard and the commit/discard workflow, so it must be the outermost builder. Because the wrapping builders type their inner as NestableBuilder, a type checker (mypy/pyright, and so any IDE) flags CacheBuilder(AtomicBuilder(...)) as it is typed; __init__ also raises at runtime, since Python type hints are not enforced. The language-neutral form of this rule — atomic is the outermost layer in the wire spec — is validated in the Rust core, so every future frontend inherits it (see docs/boundary-schema.md).

docs.title: BuildLayer
docs.text:
Hook interface for build capabilities. All hooks are optional.

Layers never touch plan structure or node state directly; they obtain results (around_node), adjust the context, and propose work through the scheduler.

docs.title: NodeContext dataclass
docs.text:
NodeContext(
    workspace_root,
    output_root,
    deletions_root=None,
    scrub=False,
)

Where one node's execution reads and writes.

Declared paths on actions are logical names; the context maps them to physical places. With no layers both roots are the workspace. The atomic layer points output_root at its staging tree and deletions_root at its deletion markers — reads then see the workspace as it will look after commit: staged outputs shadow workspace files and marked deletions hide them (the overlay).

docs.title: Workspace dataclass
docs.text:
Workspace(
    root,
    packages,
    graph,
    depends_on=dict(),
    footprints=dict(),
    patterns=dict(),
    full_load=True,
)

A loaded hierarchical workspace: its packages, their merged graph, the ownership map, and the derived cross-package dependency index. graph plugs straight into the existing builders (it is an ordinary merged Graph). owner_of maps a changed path to its package; dependents_of (the reverse of depends_on) is what a later tier will walk to load only the packages an edit touches — "package P changed → also load its dependents." Nothing consumes the index yet, so there is no staleness surface here; it is derived and (optionally) persisted for tiers 2b/3.

docs.title: dependents_of
docs.text:
dependents_of(package)

Packages that depend on package (the reverse index): if this package's files change, these must also be loaded/rebuilt.

docs.title: save_index
docs.text:
save_index(metadata_dir='build/.brix')

Persist per-package input/output patterns, footprints, and the cross-package dependency edges (repo-relative), so a later build can decide what to load without loading — or re-deriving — anything.

Merges with an existing index: entries are written for the packages this workspace actually loaded (self.patterns), entries for packages that no longer exist are dropped, and entries for discovered-but-unloaded packages are kept as-is — so a subset load refreshes its slice without clobbering the rest. last_selected records the loaded set, the recovery anchor after a failed build.

Edges are the performance-critical part. Deriving them is O(packages² × patterns), so they are computed once on a full load (where depends_on is complete and authoritative) and persisted; a later subset build reads them O(packages) instead of re-deriving. A subset save carries the persisted edges forward — sound because a subset build only happens when no brix.py changed, so patterns are stable — unless a footprint-driven reload actually changed a loaded package's input/output patterns, in which case the edges are dropped so the next build full-loads and heals them (edges depend only on the patterns).

docs.title: WorkerSpec dataclass
docs.text:
WorkerSpec(name, command_line, inputs=dict())

How to launch a worker. command_line renders (like an action's) from inputs into the worker's launch argv; name is diagnostic identity.

docs.title: build_stack
docs.text:
build_stack(
    graph_supplier,
    root=".",
    *,
    metadata_dir="build/.brix",
    cache_dir="build/.brix-cache",
    store=None,
    staging_dir="build/staging",
    detector=None,
    verify_contents=False,
    scrub=False
)

Assemble the standard builder stack in the correct order — AtomicBuilder(CacheBuilder(IncrementalBuilder(...))) — so the ordering can't be gotten wrong (atomic outermost; see NestableBuilder).

Layers toggle by argument: pass cache_dir=None (and no store) to drop the cache, staging_dir=None to drop atomic staging (e.g. a cross-module compiler that self-resolves its classpath, which atomic staging can't support — see examples/kotlin_multimodule). detector is the change-detector factory threaded to the IncrementalBuilder (e.g. GitChangeDetector); None uses the default stat detector. verify_contents=True makes the default detector re-hash every file instead of trusting its (mtime, size) cache — slower, but it catches a content change that leaves size and mtime unchanged. scrub=True runs each process with an authoritative environment (only the plumbing base plus each action's declared allowlist), so an undeclared ambient variable can't silently affect the build. Defaults give the full recommended stack.

Returns a builder; for cli.main's builder_factory (called fresh per invocation, so commit/discard rebuild cleanly), pass a thunk::

cli.main(create_graph, builder_factory=lambda: build_stack(create_graph, root=ROOT))

docs.title: load_workspace
docs.text:
load_workspace(
    root,
    *,
    brix_file="brix.py",
    graph_attr="create_graph",
    only=None
)

Discover every package under root, load each package's graph, and merge them. Returns a Workspace; ws.graph is a plain merged Graph usable with any builder — e.g.::

ws = load_workspace(ROOT)
cli.main(lambda: load_workspace(ROOT).graph, root=ROOT, ...)

only (a set of package directories) is the subset-loading primitive: only those packages' graphs are loaded and merged, for a build that touches just part of the workspace. It is deliberately mechanical — it loads exactly what it is told; deciding which packages are the affected set (so the partial build is complete, not stale) is the lazy-loading tier's job, proven by the equivalence oracle. Unselected packages' outputs are assumed already present and fresh on disk (from a prior full build). packages still lists every discovered package (for ownership); the cross-package index is derived only on a full load — a subset build consults the persisted index via load_index, never a partial re-derivation.

A package whose build file lacks graph_attr is skipped (it may be a standalone entry point that only wires cli.main, not a graph contributor).

docs.title: load_affected
docs.text:
load_affected(
    root,
    changed=None,
    *,
    brix_file="brix.py",
    graph_attr="create_graph",
    metadata_dir="build/.brix"
)

Load only the packages affected by changed (or by what git reports changed since the last build, when changed is None) — falling back to a full load_workspace whenever completeness cannot be proven.

Either way the persisted index is refreshed for every package actually loaded (Workspace.save_index merges, so a subset load never clobbers the other packages' entries), and last_selected is written at load time — before the build runs — so a build that fails midway can be recovered by the next selection.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
Typed C/C++ actions — compile, archive, link — plus a pkg-config resolver. They lower to the generic action model, so they compose with any other language in one graph, and compilation automatically tracks #include headers through the compiler's depfile. DoxygenAction runs doxygen over a project's own sources as a tracked, incremental step.

Typed C++ actions.

Strongly typed, ergonomic declarations — no magic string keys — that lower into the same generic action/data model as ExternalProcessAction when added to a graph. Raw and typed forms compose freely.

graph.add(
    cpp.CompileSourceAction(
        source_files=data.glob("src/{name}.cpp"),
        object_files=data.glob("build/obj/{name}.o"),
        compiler=data.tool("c++"),
        compile_options=["-O2", "-std=c++20"],
    ),
    cpp.LinkApplicationAction(
        object_files=data.glob("build/obj/{name}.o"),
        output_file=data.file("build/bin/app"),
        linker=data.tool("c++"),
    ),
)

docs.title: CompileSourceAction
docs.text:
CompileSourceAction(
    *,
    source_files,
    object_files,
    compiler=None,
    compile_options=None,
    deps=None
)

Bases: Action

Compile every matching source into its object file, in parallel.

Lowers to an ExpandAll over source_files whose child compiles one translation unit; source_files and object_files must share one binding name (e.g. src/{name}.cpp → build/obj/{name}.o).

docs.title: ArchiveAction
docs.text:
ArchiveAction(*, object_files, output_file, ar=None)

Bases: Action

Bundle object files into a static library with ar.

Uses ar Dcrs: Deterministic (no timestamps/uids, so the archive is byte-reproducible — its content hash is stable when the objects are, which keeps dependents from re-linking spuriously), create, replace, and build the symbol index. Link against the result by passing it as one of LinkApplicationAction's object_files (the linker pulls the members it needs).

Note on removed sources: ar updates an existing archive rather than rebuilding it. Under the atomic layer (the recommended stack) the archive is written into fresh staging each build, so a deleted source cannot leave a stale member. Without atomic, run clean after removing a source that fed the library.

docs.title: DoxygenAction
docs.text:
DoxygenAction(
    *, config, source_files, output_dir, doxygen=None
)

Bases: Action

Generate HTML API docs for a project's own C/C++ sources with doxygen.

Documentation of the user's code, run as an ordinary tracked step. doxygen is config-driven (doxygen <Doxyfile>), so unlike javadoc/typedoc there are no source arguments on the command line — the Doxyfile names the INPUT directories and the OUTPUT_DIRECTORY. brix cannot read those out of the config, so you declare both to it: source_files (the inputs, tracked so an edited header rebuilds the docs) and output_dir (which must match the Doxyfile's OUTPUT_DIRECTORY/HTML_OUTPUT, so brix tracks and stages the tree doxygen actually writes). The config file is itself an input — changing a Doxyfile setting regenerates.

::

cpp.DoxygenAction(
    config="Doxyfile",
    source_files=data.glob("src/{name}.h") + data.glob("src/{name}.cpp"),
    output_dir="build/docs/html",
)

docs.title: pkg_config
docs.text:
pkg_config(names, *, pkg_config='pkg-config')

Resolve installed system libraries via pkg-config into a DepSet: --cflags become the set's compile flags (-I/-D) and --libs its link flags (-L/-l). Feed it to CompileSourceAction(deps=...) and LinkApplicationAction(deps=...).

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Every action declares its inputs and outputs as data expressions: concrete files, globs, values, and tools. Brix infers dependency edges from where these overlap, so the data model is how you tell Brix what a step touches. In build files you usually construct them through a graph's data factory (g.data.file(...), g.data.glob(...)), documented here as DataFactory.

Logical data expressions.

These are the user-facing declarations of what data exists: files, file collections, tools, and literal values. They are clean-build truth — they say nothing about caching, staging, or incremental state.

docs.title: DataExpr
docs.text: Base class for all logical data expressions.

docs.title: DataAtom
docs.text:
Bases: DataExpr

A leaf data expression.

content_key is the atom's comparison semantics: the name of the content lens fingerprinting compares it through (e.g. "jvm-abi"). None — the default for a plain file/glob — is byte hashing. It is intrinsic to what the datum is (like the File/Tool/Value distinction), so a lens is a typed subclass (brix.java's AbiFile/AbiGlob), not a string the author types. See docs/content-key.md.

docs.title: substitute
docs.text:
substitute(bindings)

Return a copy with {name} bindings applied where meaningful.

docs.title: FileData
docs.text:
FileData(path)

Bases: DataAtom

One logical path. It need not exist yet.

Byte-hashed by default. A skin's typed subclass (brix.java.AbiFile) overrides content_key to fingerprint by meaning instead.

docs.title: GlobData
docs.text:
GlobData(pattern, exclude=())

Bases: DataAtom

A path set with optional named bindings, e.g. src/{name}.cpp.

Byte-hashed by default; a skin's typed subclass (brix.java.AbiGlob) overrides content_key to apply a content lens to every matched file.

Subtraction narrows membership: data.glob("{name}.cc") - "*_test.cc" returns a copy whose find drops files matching the fnmatch pattern(s) (*/?/[...], matched against the workspace-relative path, * crossing /). Membership only — substitution carries excludes through untouched, and the planner's edge inference ignores them (docs/content-key.md).

A path set matched by a regular expression with named groups.

Prototype support is match-only: a regex collection can drive membership but cannot be used as a substitutable output template.

docs.title: Extending brix
docs.text: Brix has three plug-in seams. Each is an injected object you pass to a builder, so a project can swap in its own behavior without touching the engine.

docs.title: Change detection
docs.text:
How Brix decides whether a file changed. The default stats and hashes on demand; GitChangeDetector accelerates a git working tree by trusting git's own view of what is unmodified. It accelerates both engines (see docs/roadmap.md).

Brix's supported Python authoring and extension API.

Engine implementation types live in their defining modules and are not part of the top-level v1 contract. See docs/python-api.md.

docs.title: GitChangeDetector
docs.text:
GitChangeDetector(root='.', metadata=None, inner=None)

Wraps a TimeAndHashChangeDetector, vouching tracked+unmodified files as unchanged without stat-ing them. Presents the same interface (the incremental and cache layers use it identically), sharing the inner detector's metadata.

Configuring this detector accelerates both engines: the Python engine uses this class directly, and on the Rust engine the builder emits a git_detection flag (see builders.py) that turns on the native mirror in rust/brix-core/src/gitdetect.rs — same vouch, same baseline/dirty metadata, so a build started on one engine continues correctly on the other.

docs.title: changed_paths
docs.text:
changed_paths()

Absolute paths changed since the last build — the working-tree diff, commits since the baseline, and the last build's dirty set (a file dirty then and clean now was reverted, which is still a change since that build). None when git cannot answer (no repo, no baseline, a git call failed): callers must treat None as "anything may have changed".

This is the enumeration query the lazy-loading tier uses to decide which packages to load, independent of any loaded graph.

docs.title: Result caching
docs.text:
Where built results are stored so they can be restored — across workspaces or across a team. Implement CacheStoreProtocol to back the cache with your own storage.

Brix's supported Python authoring and extension API.

Engine implementation types live in their defining modules and are not part of the top-level v1 contract. See docs/python-api.md.

docs.title: CacheStore
docs.text:
CacheStore(directory)

Content-addressed result store under one directory.

docs.title: restore
docs.text:
restore(fingerprint, entry, ctx)

Copy the entry's outputs to ctx.output_root. False (and no further copies) if the entry is corrupt — the caller falls back to running the process, which overwrites anything partial.

docs.title: CacheStoreProtocol
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

What CacheLayer requires of a store. Structural — a store need not subclass this, only match the three methods.

An entry is an opaque dict a store returns from load and receives back in restore; the layer only reads entry["result"] (a ProcessResult as a dict) from it. Everything else in the entry is the store's private business. restore copies the entry's cached outputs to ctx.output_root and returns whether it fully succeeded; a store may let I/O errors propagate — the layer catches them.

docs.title: HttpCacheStore
docs.text:
HttpCacheStore(
    base_url, *, auth=None, retries=2, timeout=30.0
)

Content-addressed result store backed by an HTTP GET/PUT endpoint.

docs.title: restore
docs.text:
restore(fingerprint, entry, ctx)

Fetch every blob first, then write — so a missing/failed blob is a clean miss (False) with no partial outputs left behind, matching the local store.

docs.title: store
docs.text:
store(fingerprint, result, outputs)

Upload blobs, then the entry last — so an entry is only ever visible once all its blobs are (a partial upload reads back as a miss).

docs.title: TwoTierCacheStore
docs.text:
TwoTierCacheStore(front, back)

A fast local store in front of a slower shared one.

A read checks the front first, so a local hit costs no round-trip to the back (typically a remote/team cache). A back hit is served and then promoted into the front, so the next build on this machine hits locally. A write populates the front and best-effort the back — a write to an unreachable back never blocks local caching.

Both tiers must share the entry shape used here: entry["result"] (a ProcessResult dict) and entry["outputs"] (an iterable of the logical output paths). The built-in CacheStore satisfies this; so does any store modeled on it. Promotion never touches a tier's internal blob layout — it re-stores from the files restore just wrote — so the two tiers need not share physical storage, only that entry shape.

docs.title: DepSet dataclass
docs.text:
DepSet(artifacts=(), compile_flags=(), link_flags=())

An ordered set of resolved artifact paths (jars, .a/.so) plus the flags they require. Both flag tuples are empty for a JVM classpath (the classpath is the artifacts); C++ adapters populate compile_flags (-I/-D) and link_flags (-L/-l) — separate because a -I belongs on the compile and a -l on the link.

docs.title: files
docs.text:
files()

The artifacts as byte-lens file atoms (the consumer re-lenses).

docs.title: Content lenses
docs.text:
How Brix judges whether a change actually matters to dependents — comparing a file by meaning, not bytes. Register a ContentIdentity to add your own lens; the built-in jvm-abi, kotlin-abi, and ts-dts lenses are selected by the typed helpers (java.abi, kotlin.abi, ts.dts).

Content-identity plugins: fingerprint a file by meaning, not bytes.

A ContentIdentity turns a file's bytes into a digest of some semantic identity — e.g. jvm-abi hashes a jar's API surface, not its bytes — so a dependent's fingerprint changes only when the meaning it depends on changes. This is the Python reference engine's lens computation; the lens is selected by an atom's content_key (set by a typed subclass like brix.java.AbiFile — the author writes java.abi(expr), never the name). It is opt-in per atom; the default is byte hashing. It affects fingerprint material only: what is stored, staged, restored, and compared for output-intactness still uses bytes (see docs/java-fast-builds.md and docs/content-key.md).

The versioned tag <name>@<version> is part of the fingerprint payload, so bumping a plugin's version cleanly invalidates everything it fingerprinted. Bump it on any change to extraction or normalization.

The built-ins (jvm-abi, ts-dts) are also implemented in the Rust core (rust/brix-core/src/identity.rs) so every skin gets them; the digests are cross-engine cache keys, so the Python code here remains the reference implementation, and a version bump in one implementation must land in both. A custom plugin registered here crosses the boundary as the content_identity extension trait: the engine calls its digest back per file (from build worker threads), and its digests cache in metadata.json under the same versioned tag either engine would use.

docs.title: ContentIdentity
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

A registered content-identity plugin.

docs.title: digest
docs.text:
digest(path)

The identity digest of the file. Raises on a file it cannot interpret (the engine falls back to byte hashing under a :raw tag).

docs.title: JvmAbiIdentity
docs.text: Java ABI hashing: a dependent recompiles on API changes, not on implementation-only changes. Delegates to the pure-Python parser in brix.jvmabi.

docs.title: KotlinAbiIdentity
docs.text: Kotlin ABI hashing: jvm-abi semantics, except classes whose Kotlin metadata declares inline functions/accessors (whose implementation — bodies, line tables, nested synthetics — compiles into consumers) count by whole-class bytes. Delegates to the pure-Python parser in brix.kotlinabi.

docs.title: TsDtsIdentity
docs.text: TypeScript declaration (.d.ts) hashing: a consumer recompiles on an API-surface change, not on an implementation-only change or a doc-comment edit. Delegates to the pure-Python normalizer in brix.tsdts.

docs.title: register
docs.text:
register(identity)

Register a plugin under its name (replacing any existing one).

docs.title: get
docs.text:
get(name)

Resolve a name to its plugin. Unknown names are loud — a typo in identity= must not silently degrade to byte hashing.

docs.title: tag
docs.text:
tag(identity)

The versioned fingerprint tag, e.g. jvm-abi@1.

docs.title: builtins
docs.text:
builtins()

The content-identity names the core builds in, as opposed to custom skin plugins registered later. A graph's content keys outside this set cross the engine boundary as content_identity digest callbacks.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
Typed Java actions — compilation through a warm javac worker, jar assembly, JUnit test runs — with the jvm-abi lens (abi) so a dependent recompiles only when an upstream module's public API changes, and resolver adapters (pom, maven, gradle) that adopt an existing build's classpath. JavadocAction runs javadoc over a project's own sources as a tracked, incremental step.

Typed Java actions.

Like brix.cpp, these lower into the generic action/data model when added to a graph — one underlying representation, so C++, Java, and raw process actions compose freely (a C++ tool can generate Java sources that feed a JarAction).

java.JarAction(
    source_files=(
        data.glob("src/main/java/{class_name}.java")
        + data.glob("build/generated/java/{class_name}.java")
    ),
    output_file=data.file("build/libs/app.jar"),
    entry_point="App",
)

Java compilation is inherently whole-program (javac sees every source at once), so this lowers to two actions: one javac invocation producing a classes directory, and one jar invocation packaging it.

Directory convention: the classes directory is declared as a data.file output of the javac step (so it renders through output_root and stages under atomic builds) and as a data.file input of the jar step (so it resolves through the overlay). Class-file tracking uses a bare {name}.class glob, which is recursive by default (matches across /) and so covers packaged classes (com/foo/Bar.class), not just default-package ones — a changed packaged class thus re-runs the jar step, avoiding a stale jar.

docs.title: AbiFile
docs.text:
AbiFile(path)

Bases: FileData

A jar/class compared through the JVM ABI lens, not its bytes: a dependent recompiles on an API change, not an implementation-only one. brix.java owns this lens — the core dispatches the jvm-abi name through its content-key registry (docs/content-key.md).

docs.title: AbiGlob
docs.text:
AbiGlob(pattern, exclude=())

Bases: GlobData

The glob counterpart of AbiFile: the JVM ABI lens applied to every matched jar/class.

docs.title: JarAction
docs.text:
JarAction(
    *,
    source_files,
    output_file,
    javac=None,
    jar_tool=None,
    options=None,
    classes_dir="build/classes",
    entry_point=None,
    classpath=None,
    processorpath=None,
    resource_dir=None,
    javac_worker=None
)

Bases: Action

Compile Java sources and package them into a jar.

processorpath contains annotation-processor jars. Unlike classpath, these are tracked by their complete bytes: changing processor implementation must recompile sources even when the processor's Java ABI did not change.

docs.title: JavadocAction
docs.text:
JavadocAction(
    *,
    source_files,
    output_dir,
    javadoc=None,
    options=None,
    classpath=None
)

Bases: Action

Generate HTML API docs for a project's own Java sources with javadoc.

This is documentation of the user's code, run as an ordinary tracked step — not the same thing as brix's own docs. Declaring the sources as inputs is what makes it incremental: the doc set rebuilds when a source changes and replays untouched when nothing did, like any other action.

classpath (a DepSet or list of resolved deps) is passed to javadoc so it can resolve referenced types; it is tracked through the abi lens, so an implementation-only change in a dependency lets the docs replay. Pass extra flags (-quiet, -Xdoclint:none, -link …) through options.

::

java.JavadocAction(
    source_files=data.glob("src/main/java/{name}.java"),
    output_dir="build/docs/api",
)

docs.title: JUnitTestAction
docs.text:
JUnitTestAction(
    *,
    test_sources,
    classpath,
    console_jar,
    javac_worker,
    name="junit tests",
    test_classes_dir="build/test-classes",
    test_resource_dirs=None,
    java=None,
    options=None,
    select="--scan-class-path"
)

Bases: Action

Compile JUnit 5 test sources and run them with the platform console launcher, so brix runs a suite only when its inputs actually change.

The key move is two lenses on the same classpath jars: the test compile depends on them through jvm-abi (compilation cares only about the API), while the test run depends on them through their bytes (execution cares about the implementation). So an implementation-only change to the code under test does not recompile the tests but does re-run them; a change touching nothing on a suite's classpath re-runs nothing.

The run declares no file outputs, so it replays purely on its input fingerprint: a passing suite is cached like any result (and restored on a clean checkout), while a failing suite is recorded as failed and re-runs until its inputs change.

classpath is the code under test (jars). console_jar is a junit-platform-console-standalone jar — the runner and the source of the Jupiter API the tests compile against. Tests compile through the warm javac worker (required, for the classpath join).

docs.title: pom
docs.text:
pom(
    path,
    *,
    mvn="mvn",
    scope="compile",
    cache_dir=".brix-deps",
    cwd=None
)

Adopt an existing Maven pom.xml: resolve its declared dependencies to a classpath and return it as a DepSet. The dependency declarations stay in the pom — this is the migration path (point brix at what Maven already resolves). Editing the pom re-resolves (the cache key is the pom's bytes). cwd is where Maven runs (pass the project dir when mvn is a ./mvnw wrapper); mvn may be a wrapper path like "./mvnw".

docs.title: maven
docs.text:
maven(
    coords,
    *,
    mvn="mvn",
    scope="compile",
    cache_dir=".brix-deps",
    cwd=None
)

Resolve inline Maven coordinates ("group:artifact:version") to a classpath via Maven, returned as a DepSet. The declarations live in brix.py — the greenfield / single-file path. Editing the list re-resolves. Naming the engine (maven) is deliberate: Maven and Gradle apply different version-conflict rules, so this gives Maven's resolution.

docs.title: gradle
docs.text:
gradle(
    path,
    *,
    gradle="gradle",
    configuration="compileClasspath",
    project=None,
    cache_dir=".brix-deps",
    cwd=None
)

Adopt an existing Gradle project: resolve a configuration's classpath (Gradle's compileClasspath / runtimeClasspath / testRuntimeClasspath, the analog of a Maven scope) and return it as a DepSet. This is the migration path for a Gradle build — the declarations stay in the build files; brix drives Gradle and consumes what it resolves (with Gradle's own version-conflict rules). Editing a build file re-resolves (see _GRADLE_MANIFEST_FILES for exactly which files the cache key covers).

path is the project directory (or a build script inside it). project is a Gradle project path (":service-a") to target a subproject of a multi-project build; None targets the root project. gradle may be a wrapper path like "./gradlew"; cwd is where it runs (defaults to the project dir).

docs.title: abi
docs.text:
abi(expr)

View a data expression through the JVM ABI lens: every plain file/glob atom becomes its AbiFile/AbiGlob counterpart, so fingerprints compare those files by API surface. Non-file atoms (tools, values) and atoms that already carry a lens pass through unchanged. A classpath is many jars, so this applies across an expression's atoms, not just one file.

docs.title: javac_worker
docs.text:
javac_worker(
    graph,
    *,
    java=None,
    javac=None,
    jar_tool=None,
    work_dir="build/.brix-java"
)

Add the javac worker bootstrap to graph and return its WorkerSpec.

The worker is a small in-process JavaCompiler wrapper shipped with brix; it is compiled and jarred by two plain (spawned) nodes here, so the worker jar is itself a fingerprinted, cacheable build product. Pass the returned spec to JarAction(javac_worker=...) to route module compilation through the warm worker.

Idempotent: called more than once on a graph, it adds the bootstrap only once and returns the same spec, so many JarActions share one worker jar.

docs.title: Kotlin
docs.text:
Typed Kotlin actions — compilation through a warm kotlinc worker and jar assembly — with the kotlin-abi lens (abi), which recovers the cross-module compile-skip while staying sound about inline functions (whose bodies the compiler copies into callers).

Kotlin compilation via kotlinc, mirroring brix.java.JarAction.

Two things make Kotlin different from javac and shape this module:

  1. kotlinc compiles a whole module at once. There is no per-file object; one edited source recompiles the module and rewrites every .class. That is correct, not a regression — the action declares all sources as one input set and the whole classes tree as its output.

  2. Framework classes are final by default. Spring proxies its @Configuration/@Component/@Transactional beans by subclassing them, which a final class silently defeats at run time (it compiles clean, then fails to boot). Gradle's kotlin("plugin.spring") fixes this by running the all-open compiler plugin with its spring preset, which makes classes carrying those annotations open. This module reproduces that exactly via spring_allopen= — omitting it is the trap, so the helper makes it a first-class argument rather than something you assemble by hand.

Classpath handling follows the brix.java precedent for a JVM tool that is not the warm worker (JUnitTestAction's run step): kotlinc's -classpath takes a single File.pathSeparator-joined token, so the resolved jar paths are joined into one value for the command line, while the same jars are declared as kotlin-abi-lensed fingerprint inputs so a dependency change recompiles the module exactly when it can matter.

The classpath is lensed through kotlin-abi, not the jvm-abi lens java.JarAction uses: a Kotlin inline fun copies its body — line-number tables and nested synthetic classes included — into consumers' bytecode at compile time, so the "body is not part of the interface" assumption behind jvm-abi is unsound for a consumed Kotlin module (it once let brix skip a recompile whose output had actually changed — a stale result, the worst build failure). kotlin-abi (brix/kotlinabi.py) keeps jvm-abi's skip for classes without inline members and counts inline-carrying classes by whole-class bytes, failing closed on anything it will not vouch for: implementation-only edits in inline-free classes no longer recompile dependents, and inline changes always do.

docs.text:
KotlinAbiFile(path)

A jar/class compared through the Kotlin ABI lens: jvm-abi semantics, except classes whose Kotlin metadata declares inline members (whose implementation compiles into consumers) count by whole-class bytes. brix.kotlin owns this lens — the core dispatches the kotlin-abi name through its content-key registry (docs/content-key.md).

docs.text:
KotlinAbiGlob(pattern, exclude=())

The glob counterpart of KotlinAbiFile: the Kotlin ABI lens applied to every matched jar/class.

Compile a whole Kotlin module with kotlinc and package it into a jar.

spring_allopen is the path to the distribution's allopen-compiler-plugin.jar; when given, the Spring all-open preset is applied (the equivalent of Gradle's kotlin("plugin.spring")). The plugin jar is a byte-lens input, so a kotlinc upgrade recompiles.

docs.title: abi
docs.text:
abi(expr)

View a data expression through the Kotlin ABI lens: every plain file/glob atom becomes its KotlinAbiFile/KotlinAbiGlob counterpart. Non-file atoms (tools, values) and atoms that already carry a lens pass through unchanged. Safe on mixed classpaths: a plain Java jar has no Kotlin metadata, so the lens degrades to exactly jvm-abi for it.

docs.title: kotlinc_worker
docs.text:
kotlinc_worker(
    graph,
    *,
    kotlin_compiler,
    java=None,
    javac=None,
    jar_tool=None,
    work_dir="build/.brix-kotlin"
)

Add the kotlinc worker bootstrap to graph and return its WorkerSpec.

A cold kotlinc pays JVM startup and loads/JIT-warms the whole Kotlin compiler on every call, so keeping it warm between compilations is the big edit-loop win — the Kotlin analogue of java.javac_worker. Pass the returned spec to JarAction(kotlinc_worker=...) to route module compilation through the warm worker instead of spawning kotlinc.

kotlin_compiler is the distribution's lib/kotlin-compiler.jar (the self-contained compiler the worker instantiates in-process by reflection); the worker itself is plain Java, so it compiles with javac alone. Note the compile-vs-launch JDK split: the worker is compiled with --release 17 so it runs on whatever java launches it, which must be a JDK the Kotlin compiler supports (its version, not the worker's, is what compiles your sources).

Idempotent: called more than once on a graph, it adds the bootstrap only once and returns the same spec, so many JarActions share one worker jar.

docs.title: Spring Boot
docs.text:
Assemble an executable Spring Boot "fat jar" — a repackaged jar that boots with java -jar. Builds on brix.java, so the classpath resolution and incremental compile carry over.

Spring Boot executable-jar packaging.

Builds on brix.java: it takes a plain application jar (the payload a java.JarAction already produces) plus the app's Maven-resolved runtime dependency jars, and repackages them into one executable jar via Spring's own spring-boot-loader-tools Repackager — the same code the Maven and Gradle plugins call, so the result is byte-for-byte a standard Spring Boot jar runnable with java -jar.

brix does not reimplement the BOOT-INF layout (nested BOOT-INF/lib/*.jar, the loader classes, the JarLauncher manifest); it drives Spring's repackager over a resolver-provided classpath. It does own the tracking: the plain jar and every bundled dependency are byte-lens inputs, so the executable jar re-stales whenever the app or any dependency it ships changes.

repackager = springboot.boot_repackager(
    graph, loader_tools_classpath=[...]  # from Maven, see the example
)
graph.add(java.JarAction(..., output_file=data.file("build/app.jar")))
graph.add(
    springboot.SpringBootJar(
        source_jar=data.file("build/app.jar"),
        output_file=data.file("build/app-boot.jar"),
        main_class="com.example.App",
        runtime_classpath=[data.file(j) for j in runtime_jars],
        repackager=repackager,
    )
)

brix infers the order from data overlap: the boot jar's source_jar is the JarAction's output.

docs.title: RepackagerSpec dataclass
docs.text:
RepackagerSpec(helper_jar, loader_tools_classpath)

Handle to the bootstrapped BootRepackager helper: its jar plus the spring-boot-loader-tools runtime classpath it loads reflectively. Returned by boot_repackager; passed to SpringBootJar.

docs.title: SpringBootJar
docs.text:
SpringBootJar(
    *,
    source_jar,
    output_file,
    main_class,
    runtime_classpath,
    repackager,
    java=None
)

Bases: Action

Repackage a plain application jar into a Spring Boot executable jar.

Lowers to a single process node that runs the BootRepackager helper (java -jar), which drives Spring's Repackager over the runtime classpath. Every jar path is passed as a data-substituted argument (never a baked -classpath), so the command template carries no machine-specific path and its fingerprint stays portable across machines and caches.

docs.title: boot_repackager
docs.text:
boot_repackager(
    graph,
    *,
    loader_tools_classpath,
    javac=None,
    jar_tool=None,
    work_dir="build/.brix-springboot"
)

Add the BootRepackager bootstrap (compile + jar) to graph and return its spec.

The helper is dependency-free at compile time — it loads loader-tools reflectively through a child class loader at run time — so this is two plain nodes and the helper jar is itself a fingerprinted, cacheable build product (the same shape as java.javac_worker's bootstrap). Idempotent: called more than once on a graph it adds the bootstrap only once.

loader_tools_classpath is the spring-boot-loader-tools runtime classpath (loader-tools plus its transitive jars) as resolved by Maven — brix consumes that resolution rather than reimplementing it.

docs.title: TypeScript
docs.text:
Typed TypeScript actions built on tsc, with the ts-dts lens (dts) so a dependent recompiles only on a public-declaration change, plus automatic import tracking (a --listFiles depfile) so editing a source a module imports — even outside its own tree — re-stales it. npm resolves installed node_modules packages' type declarations into a DepSet (deps=), tracked through the ts-dts lens so a dependency upgrade re-stales the compile. TypedocAction runs typedoc over a project's own sources as a tracked, incremental step.

Typed TypeScript actions.

Like brix.java and brix.cpp, these lower into the generic action/data model when added to a graph — one underlying representation, so TypeScript composes freely with the other languages (a code generator can emit .ts that feeds a ts.CompileAction; a .js bundle can feed a later step).

ts.CompileAction(
    sources=data.glob("src/{name}.ts"),
    out_dir="dist",
    options=["--module", "nodenext", "--target", "es2022", "--strict"],
)

tsc compiles a set of .ts sources into an outDir of .js (and, with declaration emit, .d.ts). The action declares the sources as inputs and the emitted .js/.d.ts as recursive {name} globs under out_dir (bare {name} matches across /, so nested modules — sub/mod.js — are tracked, not just top-level ones), so brix owns incrementality: it re-runs tsc only when a source or a tracked dependency actually changes, rather than delegating to tsc --build's own up-to-date check.

The cross-module lens. A module that type-checks against another module's built declarations declares them via dependencies= — the emitted upstream .d.ts files, viewed through the ts-dts lens (brix.ts owns this typed atom, as brix.java owns AbiFile). Because tsc's declaration emit writes only the public API, an implementation-only change upstream produces a byte-identical .d.ts and the ts-dts fingerprint is unchanged, so the dependent replays instead of recompiling — the TypeScript counterpart of the jvm-abi shortcut (docs/content-key.md). The upstream .d.ts are tracked fingerprint inputs; tsc's own module resolution locates them on disk (they sit in the upstream out_dir the dependent imports from), so no classpath-style flag is needed.

Automatic import tracking. The declared sources glob covers a module's own tree, but a TS import can reach a shared .ts outside it (a common utils/ file, an ambient .d.ts). Left undiscovered, editing that file would leave the module stale — the TS version of the C/C++ header problem. So by default (track_imports=True) brix wraps tsc in a --listFiles recorder that writes a Makefile depfile of every workspace .ts/.d.ts the compile actually read; the incremental layer scans it exactly like a cc -MMD one, so editing a deeply-imported source re-stales the compile. It is complementary to dependencies=: a declared upstream .d.ts is tracked through the ts-dts lens (impl-only upstream change → replay), and its directory is excluded from the depfile so that byte-tracking never overrides the lens; the depfile is only for the undeclared source imports the lens doesn't cover. Set track_imports=False for a bare single tsc spawn.

Scope for now: no warm compiler daemon (like brix.cpp, unlike brix.java's javac worker) and no npm/node_modules resolver (that is the ts.npm-style adapter of docs/dependencies.md, still planned). tsc is often not global; pass tsc=data.tool(".../node_modules/.bin/tsc") to point at a local install.

docs.title: DtsFile
docs.text:
DtsFile(path)

Bases: FileData

A .d.ts declaration file compared through the ts-dts lens, not its bytes: a consumer recompiles on a public-API change, not an implementation-only change or a doc-comment edit. brix.ts owns this lens — the core dispatches the ts-dts name through its content-key registry (docs/content-key.md).

docs.title: DtsGlob
docs.text:
DtsGlob(pattern, exclude=())

Bases: GlobData

The glob counterpart of DtsFile: the ts-dts lens applied to every matched .d.ts.

docs.title: CompileAction
docs.text:
CompileAction(
    *,
    sources,
    out_dir,
    tsc=None,
    options=None,
    declaration=True,
    dependencies=None,
    deps=None,
    track_imports=True,
    python=None
)

Bases: Action

Compile a module's TypeScript sources with tsc into out_dir.

Emits .js for every source and, when declaration is set (the default, so the module is usable as a dependency), a .d.ts beside each. dependencies is the list of upstream modules' built .d.ts this module type-checks against; they are tracked through the ts-dts lens, so an implementation-only change upstream lets this module replay.

docs.title: TypedocAction
docs.text:
TypedocAction(
    *, entry_points, output_dir, typedoc=None, options=None
)

Bases: Action

Generate HTML API docs for a project's own TypeScript sources with typedoc.

Documentation of the user's code, run as an ordinary tracked step: the declared entry_points (the sources) are inputs, so the doc set rebuilds on a source change and replays when nothing changed. Pass typedoc flags (--name, --excludePrivate, --tsconfig …) through options.

typedoc is usually a local install, not global; pass typedoc=data.tool(".../node_modules/.bin/typedoc") to point at it.

::

ts.TypedocAction(
    entry_points=data.glob("src/{name}.ts"),
    output_dir="build/docs/api",
)

docs.title: npm
docs.text:
npm(names, *, node_modules='node_modules', root='.')

Resolve npm packages' TypeScript type declarations into a DepSet.

brix does not run npm — you npm install and this adapter consumes the result (the java.pom/cpp.pkg_config pattern for the JS ecosystem). For each package it collects that package's .d.ts under node_modules (and @types/<name> for DefinitelyTyped packages), so upgrading a dependency whose types changed re-stales the compile.

tsc still resolves the imports off the real filesystem at compile time; these are tracked inputs, not command arguments. Pass the result as ts.CompileAction(deps=…) — the consumer applies the ts-dts lens, so a comment-only change to a dependency's .d.ts lets the module replay while a real type change rebuilds it.

Resolution reads the real filesystem now (per build, like the Maven adapters). Paths are returned relative to root (the workspace root the build runs from). Raises if a named package has no discoverable .d.ts.

docs.title: dts
docs.text:
dts(expr)

View a data expression through the ts-dts lens: every plain file/glob atom becomes its DtsFile/DtsGlob counterpart, so fingerprints compare those declaration files by public surface. Non-file atoms (tools, values) and atoms that already carry a lens pass through unchanged. A module can depend on many upstream .d.ts, so this applies across an expression's atoms.
